cover.title: Pick or skip
cover.lead: List every subset: for each value, pick it and go on, then undo it and go on without it.
cover.use_it_when: A problem asks for every group you can choose, or the best of them, and n is small.
cover.why_it_matters: Pick or skip is the first backtracking move. Permutations, combinations and grid search build on it.

slides.title: Pack a lunchbox
slides.scene: Three snacks on the table. For each one you decide: into the lunchbox, or leave it. Every set of choices makes a different box.

blocks.text: The [[empty box]] counts too: you skipped all three.

slides.title: Pick 1 first
slides.lead: Pick 1, then decide 2 and 3: four subsets. Skip 1 and the same four come again without it.

quickcheck.question: How many subsets does 1 2 3 4 have?
quickcheck.answer: Answer: {{len(subsets([1, 2, 3, 4]))}}. The 4 doubles the 8: with it or without it.

blocks.text: One list holds the picks. Removing the last pick takes you back, so the skip branch starts clean.

blog.summary: Every group you could choose: for each value, pick it and recurse, then undo the pick and recurse without it.
blog.tested_inputs: hand-picked inputs (1 2 3, one value, two values, negatives, ten values) and random sets of up to 8 distinct values from −10 to 10
blog.tested_against: a brute force that reads each subset off the bits of a counter, highest bit first, so the order matches pick-before-skip
blog.tested_extra: The pick and skip steps in the walk-through, the quick-check answer and the trap result come from running the code.

caption.first: Subsets with backtracking, explained as pick or skip: every subset of 1 2 3 in a 12-line template (LeetCode 78).
lines: For each value: pick it and go on, then remove it and go on without it. Each value doubles the count.
The trap: save picked itself instead of a copy, and all 8 saved subsets come out empty.
